Sunday. Rukmini spread her 600 rupees on the bed in three piles. “Half for the guitar fund,” she told her brother Sumit, dropping 300 into the tin. “A third for me. That's 200. The rest for Amma's birthday and the temple box.” “Seems fair,” Sumit said. “Can I get a share?” “Only from the gift pile.”
Friday, two weeks on. At the school fair Rukmini bought a bracelet for 60 rupees and felt no guilt at all; that pile was hers to spend.
A month later, on a Sunday, she opened the tin. It held 300 rupees, and the gift envelope's 100 bought a scarf for Amma and rice for the temple kitchen. Nothing felt taken away.

qa.a: Rukmini dropped 300 rupees into the tin.

qa.q: How did Rukmini feel about buying the bracelet at the fair?
qa.a: She felt comfortable and free of guilt, since that pile was hers to spend.

qa.q: What could Rukmini do if her allowance goes up or down?
qa.a: She could keep the same shares, half, a third and the rest, and recalculate the amounts, since the plan stays fair as the numbers change.

qa.q: How might Sumit see the plan?
qa.a: Sumit sees it as fair and asks for a share of the gift pile, so he seems interested and perhaps hopes for a present.

passage:
Thomas, you asked why I keep three jars on my shelf, even now. It started when I was fourteen.
My father gave me pocket money every Sunday, and I felt pulled three ways. I wanted a sewing machine, badly. I also wanted chaat with friends. And every month the mosque collected for flood families, and I felt bad putting in nothing.
So one Sunday I sat on my bed and thought it through. The machine mattered most, so half would go to that. Fun mattered too, so a third was mine to spend without guilt. And what was left, the smallest part, was for giving: Ammi's birthday, the flood box. My mother said, “Dilnaz, you've made it fair to everyone, including yourself.”
It took a year to buy the machine. But I never felt mean, or guilty, or deprived.
So your jars can be different sizes, Thomas. Just make sure all three exist.

qa.q: What did the smallest part go toward?
qa.a: Giving: Ammi's birthday and the flood box.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel before making the split?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt pulled three ways and guilty about giving nothing to the flood families.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the plan feel fair?
qa.a: Deciding a share for each want and value, the machine, fun and giving, instead of letting one crowd out the others.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz's mother have seen the three-way split?
qa.a: Dilnaz's mother seemed pleased and proud, saying the plan was fair to everyone, including Dilnaz.

grounding: An elder recalls splitting pocket money into half for a goal, a third for spending and the rest for gifts and charity, so the plan felt fair.

passage:
Madhuri's allowance had shrunk that year. The family's tailoring shop had a slow season, and Nirmala Aunty, who ran it with Madhuri's mother, said everyone was tightening. So when Madhuri got her small weekly amount, every rupee felt like it had three jobs to do.
She sat at the shop counter after closing and thought aloud to her aunt. “I want the art course in summer. That's the big one, so half goes there. I don't want to be the only one who never buys a samosa, so about a third is for me. And the rest... Diwali gifts for you and Amma, and a little for the temple's food drive.”
Nirmala Aunty raised an eyebrow. “Even the giving, when money's tight?”
“Especially when it's tight,” Madhuri said. “Otherwise it feels like money only ever goes one way.”
She wrote labels on three envelopes and tucked them under the counter drawer.

qa.q: How much of the allowance goes to the art course?
Why did Madhuri keep a share for giving even when money was tight?
qa.a: She felt it mattered to her values, not wanting to feel that money only ever went one way.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri do if the slow season continues?
qa.a: Talk with Amma and Nirmala Aunty about adjusting the shares or the course date, rather than dropping the plan.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Aunty see Madhuri's answer?
qa.a: Nirmala Aunty may be surprised and touched that Madhuri keeps room for giving in a hard year.

grounding: Shows a teen with a shrunken allowance splitting it into half for a goal, a third for spending and the rest for gifts and charity, balancing wants and values.
